source.title: Predictable Confabulations: Factual Recall by LLMs Scales with Model Size and Topic Frequency
source.authors: Matthew Smith; Jonathan P. Shock; Samuel T. Segun; I. E. Olatunji; Tegawendé F. Bissyandé

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a superposition-inspired signal-to-noise account to motivate its factual-recall scaling model, but its experiments do not measure feature overlap, polysemanticity, feature directions, or SAE recovery.
record.gate_note: The study measures scholarly-reference recall and its association with model size and topic representation; these are results about a related recall phenomenon, not direct measurements of the representational behaviors named in V1–V6. The superposition geometry and SAE findings in the related-work section are cited from other work and are not rows. The reference-generation prompt and human/automated verification results do not test a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes superposition (citing Elhage, Bricken, Templeton, Liu et al.) to motivate a signal-to-noise sigmoid for scholarly-reference recall. Its own measurements are recall quality against parameter count and OpenAlex topic counts. It measures no feature directions, overlaps, neuron polysemanticity, SAE features or feature dimensionality. A sigmoid fit consistent with an SNR story does not bear on whether any version holds; the authors say the data do not uniquely select the form. Calling it T4 is a near fit, since the study uses superposition as a premise rather than as a tool for its own method. 'assumes' with T6 would also be defensible, but the record's choice is kept.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also state the sigmoid is motivated by, not derived from, superposition, and that the data are consistent with it without uniquely selecting it. They add that the causal role of training-data frequency needs controlled pre-training experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The study generates scholarly references from LLMs and measures recall quality against model size and topic representation; it does not use the original toy-network feature-training or geometric-measurement method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports robustness to the PARTIAL relevance-score weight: across weights 0.0 to 1.0, sigmoid R2 ranges from 0.504 to 0.606 and model rank ordering has Spearman ρ ≥ 0.997. Its limitations note that a different prompt or decoding strategy could shift fitted parameters, but those alternatives were not tested.

fits_no_version.finding: Scholarly-reference recall quality across 16 dense LLMs follows a sigmoid in log parameter count and log OpenAlex topic count (R2 = 0.599; 0.604 with binary title match). Recall quality correlates positively with topic representation in 37 of 38 models. Larger models recall less-cited papers (log-log slope −0.35).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM factual recall of scholarly references scales jointly with model size and topic frequency, in a form the authors call consistent with, but not evidence of, a superposition-based interference account.

record.problems: The study is observational and cannot manipulate topic frequency independently of model capacity. OpenAlex work counts are an indirect proxy for training-data representation, and training corpora are unavailable. The task is limited to English scholarly references, the primary within-family samples are small, reported fit uncertainties assume independent residuals although clustering would widen intervals, and a coauthor has a financial interest in the verification service used.

untested.parts: All: no toy networks, sparsity sweeps or feature geometry measured.
All: capacity competition is assumed in the theory (Neff, interference floor), but neurons and features are not examined.
All: superposition in LLMs and SAE recovery are only cited (Bricken, Templeton, Liu et al.), not measured.
All: 1-D concept vectors are assumed in Eq. 2, not tested.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. They are recall-quality measures, which are a different construct from representational superposition. The R5 and R6 states (reversed and absent) refer to the topic-frequency correlation and not to any version. The superposition theory section derives predictions from assumed interference scaling. The Zipf exponent and the Liu et al. width estimates are cited or external, not tests. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more sparse features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, and sparsity-dependent geometric transitions.
Whether neurons are polysemantic because features compete for capacity, and whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for other reasons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Whether LLM features are spread across neurons or sparse features can be recovered with a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representations.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: 16 dense models across Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and Mistral (aggregate fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit factual recall quality against parameter count across dense models.
rows.measure: Log-linear fit of factual recall quality against parameter count
rows.note: Aggregate fit across the stated 16 dense models; the paper reports systematic offsets between model families.

rows.subject: 28 dense and MoE models (aggregate fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit factual recall quality against total parameter count across dense and MoE models.
rows.measure: Log-linear fit of factual recall quality against total parameter count
rows.note: Aggregate fit; the authors interpret the trend as consistent with total parameters dominating the noise floor.

rows.subject: 16 dense models across Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and Mistral (aggregate fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a sigmoid to model-topic recall-quality observations using parameter count and topic work count.
rows.uncertainty: Reported parameter errors; all |t| > 11, p ≈ 0. Authors state standard errors assume independent model-topic residuals and clustering would widen intervals.
rows.note: The fitted relation uses parameter count and OpenAlex topic work count as predictors; it does not measure representational geometry.

rows.subject: 38 tested models (aggregate correlation count)
rows.operation_detail: Measure per-model Spearman correlation between recall quality and log10 topic representation.
rows.measure: Direction of per-model Spearman correlation between quality and log10 S
rows.value: 37 of 38 models have a positive correlation; median ρ = 0.55
rows.note: The paper reports an aggregate count and median, not individual correlations for all models.

rows.subject: Grok 3
rows.operation_detail: Measure correlation between recall quality and log10 topic representation.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between quality and log10 S
rows.note: Identified by the paper as the single outlier among the 38 models.

rows.subject: DeepSeek V4 Pro
rows.operation_detail: Measure correlation between recall quality and log10 topic representation.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between quality and log10 S
rows.note: The authors say this near-zero correlation is consistent with ceiling compression.

rows.subject: 16 dense models across Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and Mistral (aggregate fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a sigmoid using binary exact-title match for real papers instead of the continuous quality score.
rows.baseline: Continuous authenticity × relevance score fit: R2 = 0.599
rows.note: The paper reports this as a robustness check and says the fit is similar to the continuous-score fit.

rows.subject: 10 dense models across four families (aggregate fit)
rows.operation_detail: Relate median citation count of correctly recalled references to model size.

conditions.value: SourceVerify verified or verified-with-error, matched to a unique OpenAlex record

rows.measure: Weighted log-log slope of median citation count against model size
rows.uncertainty: Per-model median 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; 10,000 resamples
rows.note: Aggregate trend: larger models recalled papers with lower median citation counts.
